quality_notes:
Curious Refuge Labs review scored Ray 3.2 at 7.7/10 overall: Prompt Adherence 8.1/10, Temporal Consistency 7.5/10, Visual Fidelity 7.5/10, Motion Quality 7.8/10, Style & Cinematic Realism 7.6/10. Strongest at prompt adherence, especially for structured, specific direction and realistic scenarios (ambience screens are a standout; nine of seventeen tests scored 9/10). Excels at landscapes, controlled hero shots, and wide frames with natural textures and controlled lighting. Weaknesses: drops specific fine details (e.g. missed a finger touching a chain), struggles with cartoon/fantasy physics (3D Characters Talking ignored the brief), and complex physics such as VFX explosions (6/10) where blast, smoke, and soldier movement compete for consistency. Notable artifacts: vanishing characters (a 3D hockey character gets "sucked into" the frame; a chef fades out of the 2D diner scene; a cup hangs in mid-air ignoring gravity), unintended slow motion in the shadowboxing shot, and slight character drift/stock-footage feel in crowd scenes. Visual complexity—not just amount but type—is where the model cracks.

---

Curious Refuge Labs™ review scored it 7.7/10 overall (Prompt Adherence 8.1, Temporal Consistency 7.5, Visual Fidelity 7.5, Motion Quality 7.8, Style & Cinematic Realism 7.6). Strongest at prompt adherence, especially ambience screens — the closest any model has come to nailing them — and structured, specific direction. Visual fidelity and consistency are highest on wide frames, natural textures and controlled lighting (landscapes, commercial hero shots, ambience screens all score 9). Weaknesses: complex physics and animated / cartoon-style content break down — the 3D hockey character gets "absorbed" into the frame and vanishes, the 2D diner chef fades out of frame, a 2D frog's held cup floats ignoring gravity. VFX explosions (score 6) look flat, lacking depth, debris and shockwave weight. Failed to render a specific beat (index finger touching a gold chain); it also rewrote the 3D animated command-center scene on its own terms. Shadowboxing shot was pulled into slow motion when the prompt didn't ask for it. Style & Cinematic Realism section header lists 7.33/10 but the body reports 7.6/10 and the summary table lists 7.6/10. Verdict: recommended for AI video artists, a clear step forward from Ray 3.14, but below Seedance 2.0 and Kling 3.0.
notes:
Image-to-video model (fal-ai/luma-dream-machine/ray-2/image-to-video). Cost per video: $0.50 for a 5-second clip at 540p (equivalent to $0.10/second); 9-second clips scale proportionally. Resolution options: 540p, 720p (2x base cost), 1080p (4x base cost). Six aspect ratios: 16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4, 21:9, 9:21. Supports both single-image animation and dual-image interpolation via image_url and end_image_url parameters (keyframe control). Optional loop parameter for seamless infinite playback. Input formats: JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, AVIF via URL or upload. Output: MP4 video. Commercial use permitted via fal partnership. Competitors: Luma Dream Machine Image to Video ($0.05), Kling Video v2.6 Pro ($0.25), Pixverse v5.5 ($0.10).

---

Generate continuous clips up to 20 seconds long; multiple resolutions from Draft (360p) up to full 1080p; multi-keyframe support with up to 16 control points per clip; follows up to 8 faces at once while preserving expressions and body language; native HDR and 16-bit EXR output for clean compositing; video-to-video transformation preserving lighting, movement, and performance. Positioned as a tool for directors, not just prompters. A clear step forward from Ray 3.14, but has not quite reached the level of Seedance 2.0 or Kling 3.0. Recommended for AI video artists, especially those who write structured, specific prompts and think in shot lists.
